title: Two Old Antibiotics Together Reverse Isoniazid Resistance in Drug-Resistant TB, IISc Study Finds
excerpt: Pairing isoniazid with vancomycin restored the frontline drug's power against resistant strains in patient-derived samples and mice — laboratory evidence the authors say now warrants a clinical trial.
body:
• Researchers at the Indian Institute of Science (IISc), Bengaluru, found that pairing isoniazid with vancomycin reversed isoniazid resistance in drug-resistant tuberculosis bacteria, in laboratory tests on patient-derived strains and in mice.
  • The combination cut bacterial growth by more than 90% in 14 of 16 drug-resistant clinical strains tested, and reduced the bacterial load in infected mice roughly tenfold over 10 days of treatment, where neither drug worked on its own.
  • This is laboratory and animal evidence only — no patient has been treated with the combination, and it changes nothing about TB treatment today. The authors say the results make the pairing suitable for a clinical trial in isoniazid-resistant and multidrug-resistant TB.

Two old antibiotics, each ineffective on its own against the bacteria tested, worked together to reverse drug resistance in tuberculosis, researchers at the Indian Institute of Science (IISc) in Bengaluru have reported. In a study published in the journal Microbiology Spectrum, the team showed that vancomycin — an antibiotic already in clinical use for other bacterial infections — restored the killing power of isoniazid, a frontline anti-TB drug, against drug-resistant strains of Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

The finding matters because isoniazid resistance quietly undermines the standard TB regimen. Isoniazid is a prodrug: the bacterium's own catalase-peroxidase enzyme, KatG, activates it, and the activated drug then blocks production of mycolic acids, which the bacterium needs to build its cell wall. The commonest resistance mutations strike exactly that machinery — in the katG gene or the inhA promoter — leaving the frontline drug with nothing to act on.

What the team tested

The study, led by researchers from IISc's Department of Biochemistry and Centre for Infectious Disease Research with the National Tuberculosis Institute in Bengaluru, worked with drug-resistant clinical isolates taken from patient sputum samples. Of 19 strains selected, 16 could be analysed. The set covered high-level isoniazid resistance, low-level resistance and multidrug-resistant (MDR) profiles.

In laboratory cultures, 14 of the 16 strains showed a reduction of more than 90% in growth under the isoniazid-vancomycin combination relative to at least one of the drugs alone — which the authors calculate as roughly 87% of the drug-resistant strains tested being uniquely susceptible to the combination. The team then moved to animals: mice infected with an MDR strain received isoniazid, vancomycin, both, or neither for 10 consecutive days. Isoniazid alone left lung bacterial loads high and vancomycin alone produced only a non-significant reduction, but the combination produced a significant tenfold decrease in lung bacterial load compared with every other group, a similar tenfold reduction in the spleen, and fewer of the granulomas that mark TB lung damage.

"Our study demonstrates that vancomycin, in combination with isoniazid, reverses isoniazid resistance and is effective in killing drug-resistant Mtb."

— Pal et al., Microbiology Spectrum

Why the pairing may work

The authors' explanation is tentative — in their words, the effect is "possibly due to" changes the drugs trigger in the bacterial cell wall and stress responses. Their gene-expression analysis found that isoniazid exposure switched down a set of genes involved in making PDIM, a lipid in the mycobacterial outer membrane, which they say provides a possible basis for vancomycin penetrating the bacterium more effectively once isoniazid has acted. The work builds on the group's earlier laboratory finding that isoniazid-resistant bacteria evolve a diminished capacity to counter oxidative stress, leaving them sensitive to drugs that disturb that balance.

The burden the work is aimed at

The paper frames the search against the global drug-resistant TB burden it cites from the World Health Organization's 2022 report: an estimated 410,000 incident cases of MDR TB in 2022, and an estimated 160,000 MDR TB deaths out of 1.3 million TB deaths that year. The WHO's Global Tuberculosis Report 2025 put India at 25% of the world's TB cases in 2024, the largest national share, and recorded drug-resistant TB treatment success at 71%, against 88% for drug-susceptible TB — the gap a resistance-reversing combination would need to close.

What this does not yet mean

No patient has received this combination, and the study reports no human dose, safety or side-effect data; the doses used were in mice. Vancomycin is an approved drug for other infections, including MRSA, which is part of its appeal as a repurposing candidate, but approval for one use is not evidence of benefit in TB. The authors conclude the combination is suitable for a clinical trial in isoniazid-resistant and MDR TB cases; no trial details — phase, sponsor or start date — are given in the paper. Until such a trial reads out, TB treatment is unchanged, and anyone on a TB regimen should complete it as prescribed rather than draw conclusions from a laboratory result. The full paper is available open access via its DOI record.
nri_angle: India carries 25% of the world's TB cases; a resistance-reversing pairing of two existing drugs is directly relevant to Indian families and to diaspora readers following Indian public-health research.
